Justified
JUS-ti-fide
v. (past part.)
From Latin justificare, to make or declare righteous, from justus (righteous) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: pronounced or regarded as just; absolved from guilt. In Scripture the word is forensic — a verdict pronounced by the Judge, not a quality infused into the defendant.

Biblical Definition

Justified is the Bible’s word for the sinner’s standing declared righteous before God. It is a courtroom word, not a hospital word: the Judge does not repair the guilty man and then acquit him, He acquits him on the ground of another’s righteousness imputed. Paul states the ground and the instrument in one breath: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24). Freely excludes price paid by the sinner; by his grace excludes merit; through the redemption names the price that was in fact paid, and it was paid by Christ. The instrument by which the sinner receives this verdict is faith alone: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). Peace is not a feeling produced by the verdict but the state created by it — the war is over because the charge is gone. The verdict is unbreakable because it is one link in a chain God Himself forged: whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Not one justified man falls out between the second link and the third. And the verdict falls on the unlikeliest: after cataloguing fornicators, idolaters, thieves and drunkards, Paul writes, And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines JUSTIFIED as pronounced or regarded as just; absolved from guilt or the charge of sin; freed by pardon; vindicated. Webster notes the theological sense explicitly: in the scriptural sense, freed from the penalty of sin and accepted as righteous on account of the merits of Christ.

expand to see more

JUSTIFIED, pp. — Proved or shown to be just; vindicated; cleared from blame.

Absolved from guilt; freed by pardon from the penalty due to sin.

In theology, accounted or accepted as righteous before God, not on the ground of personal obedience, but on account of the merits and righteousness of Christ received by faith.

Distinguished from sanctified: the one is a change of state before the law, the other a change of nature within the man.

From Latin justus, just, and facio, to make — the root also of justice, justify, and injustice.

Key Scripture

Romans 3:24 — "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:"

Romans 5:1 — "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:"

Romans 8:30 — "Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

Titus 3:7 — "That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life."

Modern Corruption

The Council of Trent anathematized the doctrine that justification is a declared verdict received by faith alone, and modern reconstructions of Paul have revived the substance of that denial by making justification a statement about who belongs to the covenant community rather than how a guilty man is acquitted.

expand to see more

Rome’s error is precise and it has never been withdrawn. Trent’s sixth session defined justification as a translation from a state of sin to a state of grace by means of infused righteousness, increased by good works and lost by mortal sin, and its canons pronounced anathema on anyone teaching that the sinner is justified by faith alone or that the righteousness by which he is justified is the righteousness of Christ imputed. That is not a difference of emphasis with the Reformation; it is the denial of Romans 3:24 and Romans 5:1 at the point where they are clearest. If justification is a process rather than a verdict, no man can have peace with God in this life, because no man knows whether the process is complete — which is exactly the pastoral misery the Reformation delivered the church from.

The newer corruption wears Protestant clothes. Recent reconstructions of Paul relocate justification from the courtroom to the question of covenant membership: the doctrine is said to answer not how can a guilty man stand before God but who counts as belonging to the people of God, and the imputation of Christ’s active obedience is set aside as a category the apostle never used. But Romans 8:30 chains justification to predestination on one side and glorification on the other — it is an act of God upon an individual sinner in eternity’s ordering, not a social marker. And 1 Corinthians 6:11 names fornicators, idolaters and drunkards as the men justified, which is a statement about guilt removed, not about a boundary line redrawn.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dikaioo (G1344), to declare righteous, to acquit; dikaiosis (G1347), the act of acquittal; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; Hebrew tsadaq (H6663), to be just, to be declared in the right.

expand to see more

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to pronounce just; used forensically of a judge’s verdict (Romans 3:24, 5:1, 8:30).

Greek dikaiosis (G1347) — the act of acquittal; raised again for our justification (Romans 4:25).

Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; the standing conferred, imputed to the believer (Romans 4:6).

Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be right, to be declared in the right; the judge who justifieth the wicked is an abomination (Proverbs 17:15) apart from a satisfaction.

Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to impute; the accounting term behind counted unto him for righteousness (Romans 4:3).

Usage

"Being justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24) — the ground of the verdict is grace, not the sinner’s improvement."

"Justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1) — the verdict creates the peace, not the reverse."

"Whom he justified, them he also glorified (Romans 8:30) — the chain from which no justified man is lost."
